title: Browser-Based AI Tools vs Installed Apps: How to Decide
description: Where the tool lives changes everything: privacy, offline use, integrations, and updates. A practical guide to choosing between web and installed AI tools.
author: AIVOXFLOW Editorial
disclosure: Desk research based on commonly documented capabilities of major AI platforms as of 2026-10-15. Features vary by vendor and change frequently — verify on official sites.
body:
Most major AI assistants now ship in both forms: a website and an installed app. The choice is not cosmetic: it changes what the tool can reach, what happens offline, and how your data flows.

## What the browser version does well

- **Zero install:** nothing to update, works on shared or locked-down machines
- **Always current:** the newest features usually land on the web first
- **Clean separation:** when you close the tab, the session ends; nothing lingers in an OS-level process

The limits are equally real: no deep OS integration (no system-wide hotkeys, no file-watcher automations), and tab discipline becomes your privacy strategy.

## What installed apps add

- **System integration** — global shortcuts, drag-and-drop from the desktop, context-menu actions
- **Filesystem access** — folders, terminals, developer tools; coding assistants are dramatically more useful here
- **Background features** — scheduled tasks and always-on helpers that a tab cannot offer
- **Offline or degraded modes** — some apps keep limited functionality without a connection

The costs: a larger trust surface (the app sees more of your machine), update management, and background processes on your battery.

## The decision checklist

Ask four questions:

1. **Does it need to touch my files or system?** Coding, large document sets, and OS automation favor installed apps. Q&A and drafting are fine in a tab.
2. **How sensitive is what I paste?** On a shared or work-managed device, the browser's session isolation is often safer than leaving app sessions logged in.
3. **Do I need it offline?** If yes, verify offline capabilities on the official docs: "works offline" claims deserve a specific check.
4. **Can my machine carry it?** AI desktop apps have grown heavy. If the machine is older, the web version may simply be the saner choice.

## A hybrid that works for most people

Keep the browser version as your default — it is the lowest-commitment form of the tool — and install the app only when a specific capability (file access, shortcuts, coding) justifies the trust and resource cost. Uninstall when the reason disappears.
